blocks.content: Every app needs to store data, but different apps have different needs. For example, a food delivery app tracking live orders is very different from a blogging platform storing articles.
Because of this, there are many types of databases, each designed for specific use cases. The choice of database affects your system’s performance, scalability, and complexity.
This chapter gives you a basic overview. Later, we’ll explore concepts like transactions and data modeling in more detail.

A database is software that stores, organises, and retrieves data. But not all data looks the same a user's bank transactions look nothing like a social graph or a product catalogue. Different database types are built to solve different data problems.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785282612689-84967731.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing different data shapes (structured, flexible, connected, specialised) each mapping to a different database category

blocks.content: Choosing the right database type is one of the first decisions in any system design. The wrong choice doesn't break the system but it makes everything harder: queries are slower, scaling is painful, and the data model fights you.
1. Why So Many Database Types Exist
blocks.text: 1. Why So Many Database Types Exist

blocks.content: At first, most applications used a single type of database relational databases. They were reliable, structured, and worked well for things like user data or transactions.
But as applications became more complex, new needs started to appear:

["Different data shapes: Not all data fits neatly into tables (e.g., JSON, graphs, logs)","Performance needs: Some systems need super fast reads, others need heavy writes or real-time processing","Feature-specific problems: Search engines, recommendation systems, and analytics require specialized storage","Scalability challenges: Modern apps need to handle millions of users and massive data"]
items: Different data shapes: Not all data fits neatly into tables (e.g., JSON, graphs, logs)
Performance needs: Some systems need super fast reads, others need heavy writes or real-time processing
Feature-specific problems: Search engines, recommendation systems, and analytics require specialized storage
Scalability challenges: Modern apps need to handle millions of users and massive data

blocks.content: Because of this, different database types were built each optimized for a specific problem.
Today, instead of one database doing everything, systems often use the right tool for each job.
2. The Database Ecosystem

3. Relational Databases (RDBMS)
Relational databases organize data into structured tables made up of rows and columns.
They rely on SQL (Structured Query Language) to read and manipulate data, and they enforce predefined schemas that specify how the data should be structured.
Connections between different tables are maintained using foreign keys.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129490-916121366.png
["The users table stores user details (id, name, email).","The orders table stores orders, and each order has a user_id.","The user_id in orders acts as a foreign key, linking each order to a user."]
items: The users table stores user details (id, name, email).
The orders table stores orders, and each order has a user_id.
The user_id in orders acts as a foreign key, linking each order to a user.

blocks.content: So, one user can have multiple orders, and you can use a JOIN query to fetch a user along with all their orders in one go.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785282615586-30632703.png
blocks.alt: Diagram of a relational Users table and Orders table linked by a user_id foreign key, joined by a JOIN query into combined results

blocks.content: Use when: data has clear relationships, you need complex queries, or the system handles money. PostgreSQLis the default starting point for most products.
4. Key-value stores

The simplest model. A key maps directly to a value like a giant hashmap running on a server. You can store anything as the value. You retrieve it only by its exact key. No querying by field, no joins, no aggregations.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129490-730812544.png
This diagram explains how a key-value store works using real-world examples:
["Data is stored as key → value pairs (like a dictionary).","Each key is unique, and you retrieve data directly using that key."]
items: Data is stored as key → value pairs (like a dictionary).
Each key is unique, and you retrieve data directly using that key.

blocks.content: Examples:
["Session data → session:user441abc stores user info + expiry","Cache data → cache:product:789 stores product details","Rate limiting → ratelimit:ip:103.21.1.5 stores request count"]
items: Session data → session:user441abc stores user info + expiry
Cache data → cache:product:789 stores product details
Rate limiting → ratelimit:ip:103.21.1.5 stores request count

blocks.content: Key idea:
["No complex relations or joins","Super fast lookups (O(1)) because you directly access data by key"]
items: No complex relations or joins
Super fast lookups (O(1)) because you directly access data by key

blocks.content: In short: Key-value stores are simple, fast, and perfect for caching, sessions, and quick lookups.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129797-664314149.png
Use when: caching DB query results, storing sessions, counting rate limits, or any pattern where you always know the exact key.Redisis the go-to.
5. Document databases

Data is stored as JSON-like documents. Each document is self-contained it can hold nested arrays and objects. Different documents in the same collection can have completely different fields. Schema is flexible by design.

6. Wide-column stores

Rows can have different columns and data is stored column-by-column on disk rather than row-by-row. This makes reading specific columns across billions of rows extremely fast. Built from the ground up for horizontal scale.

7. Graph databases

Data is stored as nodes (entities) and edges (relationships between them). Relationships are first-class stored directly, not computed via joins. Traversing many hops through connected data is where graph DBs dramatically outperform relational ones.

blocks.content: 10. Real systems use multiple types
Most production systems aren't picking one database they're picking several, each doing what it does best. This is called polyglot persistence.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399129799-837238240.png
Different parts of an application have very different requirements, and trying to solve all of them with a single database usually leads to compromises.

For example, the way you store user account data is very different from how you handle search queries or real-time activity logs. A single database might handle one of these really well, but it will struggle or become inefficient at scale.
That’s why modern architectures use multiple databases, each chosen based on the type of problem it solves best.

For transactional data like payments or orders, you need strong consistency and reliability, so a relational database is preferred. But for features like search, you need fast text matching, ranking, and filtering, which requires a completely different kind of system optimized for indexing, not transactions.
Similarly, for high-speed access to frequently used data, systems rely on in-memory stores.

These are designed for low latency and high throughput, making them ideal for caching and session management. Without this layer, every request would hit a slower database, increasing response time and system load.
On the other hand, if you're dealing with massive streams of data like user activity, logs, or analytics events you need a system optimized for high write throughput and horizontal scaling.
These systems are built to handle large-scale distributed workloads, often trading off some consistency for better availability and performance.
The key idea is “use the right tool for the right job.” No single database is perfect for everything.
By combining specialized systems, you get better performance, scalability, and efficiency, but at the cost of added complexity in managing and coordinating multiple data stores.
